#832. A rivalry that changed football

Brazil's Kaka had just won the 2007 Fifa Player of the Year award but it was an awkward on-stage moment next to him that was to go viral and provide perhaps the first glimpse of a generational rivalry.

A youthful Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo had finished second and third respectively but Brazil legend Pele mistakenly handed the latter the trophy for second place at the Zurich Opera House.

Fifa president Sepp Blatter had to intervene to ask the duo to swap the trophies, with both looking suitably unimpressed.

For the next 10 years, Messi or Ronaldo won every Ballon d'Or and Fifa award going. In fact since 2007, 20 of the 29 gongs awarded for Europe's player of the year has gone to one of them.

With approaching 2,000 career goals between them, 85 trophies for club and country and countless individual awards and records, Messi and Ronaldo will forever be remembered as two of the most decorated players in history.

It is a rivalry that has defined the last two decades of football, transcending clubs, countries and competitions to reshape how the game has been played, consumed and debated across the world.

"Two players like them, competing at that level for so many years, fighting over the Ballon d'Or and scoring that many goals... I don't think we'll see it again," Argentina World Cup winner Angel di Maria, who played with both, says in BBC Sport's new documentary Rivals: Messi v Ronaldo.

Driven by a pursuit of trophies, records and a relentless desire to be the best, the pair have pushed each other to new heights.

It is a rivalry that goes beyond the ultimate 'greatest of all time' debate they have fuelled.

"They both changed football," says Di Maria.

Watch the trailer for Rivals: Messi v Ronaldo

Ask anyone who is the greatest and agreement is hard to find.

"It has to be Ronaldo," ex-Manchester United team-mate Rio Ferdinand says.

"Messi is the best there has ever been," insists ex-Barcelona player and manager Xavi.

Ronaldo has had his say in the past, stating in 2012: "You cannot compare a Ferrari with a Porsche. It is a different engine. Some people say I am better, some people say he is. They are going to decide who is better in the moment and I think it's me."

What do the numbers tell us? If it's judged on goals or Champions League trophies, Ronaldo leads the way. If it's Ballons d'Or or total trophies, Messi shades it.

For some, Ronaldo nudged ahead when he helped Portugal lift the European Championship in 2016, but Messi has since guided Argentina to two Copa America titles and a World Cup.

"For me, Messi is the best player in history and Cristiano is the greatest goalscorer in history," says Spanish football expert Guillem Balague, who has written biographies of both players.

And Deco, who played with Ronaldo for Portugal and Messi for Barcelona, says: "They are special. They are totally different from the rest. It's not normal to be on this level all these years.

"Each year, there's a lot of players who do amazing things for a few years, but being almost 20 years is not normal."

Perhaps the beauty of the GOAT debate is that it may never be settled - and does not need to be.

"They have come to appreciate each as the co-stars of the football drama they have appeared in for the last 20 years," says Jonathan Clegg, co-author of a Ronaldo and Messi book.

The pair are seen by many as polar opposites.

The dribbler against the physical specimen. The shy genius against the arrogant ego. Pep Guardiola's Barcelona against Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid. Adidas against Nike.

But, while the narrative of their rivalry was undoubtedly built on their differences, the similarities between the two were striking - even from an early age.

Both players were raised in humble surroundings. Both left their homes at an early age to pursue their dreams - Messi to Barcelona from Argentina at 13 and Ronaldo to Lisbon from Madeira aged 12 - and both struggled with home sickness after leaving their family behind.

Wall Street Journal reporter Joshua Robinson, co-author of a Messi Ronaldo book, said: "Messi and Ronaldo are always portrayed as being so different but the things that forged them in their childhoods were incredibly similar.

"They both go to a place that says 'we will take your talent and make you even greater'. That promise feels appealing but is a huge gamble. That moment of total commitment is when they realise this isn't kid stuff any more. 'If I'm going to be the greatest of all time, this is where it begins.'"

But the biggest thing that brought the pair together was their unshakeable desire to succeed as they quickly built reputations as prodigious young talents.

"You could already see something different with Messi," said Xavi. "Not only the quality but the intensity with which he did things. There was an aggressiveness in attack that I had never seen before.

"Cristiano even gave him an extra push to be a better player."

Meanwhile in England, a teenage Ronaldo was signing for Manchester United from Sporting.

"I never met a young player so confident in knowing what he wanted," said Rene Meulensteen, who was part of the club's backroom team at the time. "The moment he came to Man United it was just a logical step of what he wanted to become - the best player in the world.

"Cristiano was a fast learner. I wanted to turn him from someone who could score a goal to a goalscorer. I made a three-minute video that just showed him scoring goals and also then the opportunities he didn't score. He embraced everything."

Fast forward to 2008 and the Champions League semi-final. Manchester United v Barcelona. Ronaldo v Messi for the first time.

"You could see already Messi was the best in La Liga and Cristiano was the best in the Premier League," said Spanish football journalist Guillem Balague. "To see those two kids on the pitch together was the sign of something to come."

Manchester United went on to win the trophy, Ronaldo lifted the Ballon d'Or and a rivalry for the ages had just begun.

Watch on BBC iPlayer from 06:00 BST on Friday, 5 June

"There is no doubt being in the same league changed everything," says Txiki Begiristain, director of football at Barcelona between 2003 and 2010.

Ronaldo's world record Â£80m move to Real Madrid in 2009 thrust the pair right into the centre of one of football's most intense club rivalries - Barcelona v Real Madrid.

And by the time Ronaldo left for Juventus in 2018, the pair had won five Ballons d'Or apiece. In the nine seasons the pair were together in Spain, Ronaldo had scored 450 goals in 438 games for Real. Messi, 471 in 476 games for Barca.

But it had become far more than just numbers. By now, it was personal - and the growth of social media meant the world was watching.

"For Cristiano it was Lionel Messi and for Lionel Messi it was Cristiano. 'I need to beat this guy'," said Begiristain.

"The Mourinho - Guardiola rivalry was like a mirror for the Ronaldo - Messi rivalry. And, as players, they knew that game-winning goals were their route to one-upmanship," added Spanish football writer Sid Lowe.

"We could watch it all on our phones. And in turn, the global exposure for the Messi - Ronaldo rivalry was now sky high, absolutely off the charts. Everything they did was must-see.

"It was on everyone's lips in the press box, newspapers and social media comments, Cristiano and Leo were hell bent on outdoing each other on the pitch. Their personal battle for supremacy was symbolised by the ongoing trophy battle between the clubs."

And what a battle it was. Messi and Barcelona undoubtedly won the La Liga honours, but the Champions League was dominated by Real Madrid and Ronaldo.

In 2012, Ronaldo inspired Real to their first La Liga title in four years but it was Messi who picked up his fourth straight Ballon d'Or award - much to his rival's disgust. He went to win four of the next five.

"There is a genuine animosity that begins to grow," says Robinson. "They didn't acknowledge each other that much, they hated comparisons.

"They could not tolerate if they were the greatest of all time, there could be another in their era, in their football league."

Deco adds: "I don't think there is something similar to what happened with Messi and Ronaldo at this moment because at the same time the two clubs, Barcelona and Madrid, were at the same level and fighting for the big trophies."

When Messi scored a 92nd-minute winner for Barcelona at Real Madrid in 2017, he removed his jersey and held it up the crowd.

"In the popular narrative, Cristiano had been the diva and Messi had been the humble servant of Barcelona, but this was the moment of Messi reasserting himself on the rivalry, saying maybe for the first time in his career 'look at me'," says Robinson.

Just a few months later, Ronaldo mimicked the celebration when he scored in the Spanish Super Cup at Barcelona.

Balague added: "If you needed proof of how much it meant to beat each other, those are the pictures."

The Messi v Ronaldo rivalry in Spain may have ended when the latter joined Juventus in 2018 - but the global, ongoing debate wasn't disappearing.

Ronaldo went on to return to Manchester United before moving to current club Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia, while Messi moved to Paris St-Germain, before signing for Inter Miami in America's Major League Soccer - where he remains now.

Having seen their impact in Spain, for the first time the players' moves were as commercially motivated as they were for football reasons.

"Brand Beckham opened the door for what was possible and these two have kicked the door off its hinges," said Rob Pilgrim, head of sport at Meta for Europe, Middle East and Africa.

Italian football expert Mina Rzouki, added: "You are not buying sporting excellence, you are buying a whole one-man economy."

The numbers are astronomical and the rivalry continued.

In 2018, Ronaldo joins Juventus and sells 520,000 shirts in the first 24 hours. In 2021, Messi moves to Paris and shifts 150,000 shirts in just seven minutes.

Manchester United welcome Ronaldo back in 2021, and United's total sales of his shirt (Â£187m) are almost double those of Messi's at PSG.

On Instagram, Ronaldo has close to 700m followers, Messi has 500m. The most-liked picture in the history of that platform is the Argentine lifting the World Cup trophy, amassing more than 75m likes.

Financially, Ronaldo comes out on top - according to official channels anyway. The Portuguese has topped the Forbes Money List as the world's highest paid athlete for a fourth consecutive time, with $300m (Â£223m) in total earnings. Messi is third on the list with $140m (Â£104m).

The rivalry between the pair is only accentuated by the fact they are on either side of the sportswear rivalry. Messi with Adidas and Ronaldo with Nike.

"They have become enormous global brands and what is amazing about them is they have to say almost nothing to become the world's biggest pitch man," said Robinson.

Brands the world over threw unparalleled amounts of money to get the superstars on board.

And who could forget the iconic image before the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, with both footballers playing chess against each other on a Louis Vuitton suitcase, to launch the designer's latest campaign.

"It is known as the picture that broke the internet. It was a commercial masterstroke," said Melanie Ropp, from social media marketing company the Goat Agency. "The timing of it before the World Cup made it globally iconic."

Robinson said: "Messi has nothing left to conquer. He has that one thing Ronaldo does not, a World Cup."

And, after following the Argentine in announcing his retirement from international football, it appears the global prize will continue to elude Ronaldo.

"Now the question is did Messi win this entire era of football?" adds Robinson.

#831. Football: German coach Hürzeler flying high in Premier League

Fabian Hürzeler is younger than his star player, a fellow Premier League German. But, contrary to his reputation in his homeland, Hürzeler has become a popular figure both on and off the pitch in England.

"We are absolutely in love with him. He's been an incredible manager. The results are extraordinary and we're flying."

Those words from Ben Parker will be familiar to fans of any club who have been on the kind of winning run Brighton and Hove Albion are currently on.

But all the signs on and off the pitch suggest that the man in question — Brighton's German coach Fabian Hürzeler — is more than just a flash in the Premier League pan.

Hürzeler has never coached in Germany's Bundesliga. After winning promotion to Germany's top flight with St. Pauli in 2024, he left to become the youngest man ever to take charge in England's Premier League at 31. His team currently sit third, having won six games in a row including a 5-0 thrashing of bitter rivals Crystal Palace last weekend.

It was the repeat of a fixture last season that marked Hürzeler's lowest Brighton ebb, with a 1-0 home loss making it one win in 12. "There are only two options," the German coach said at the time. "Give up or keep pushing harder, and that's always the option I choose in my life."

Parker, the co-editor of Brighton and Hove Albion fanzine, Dogma, admitted to DW that there were plenty who weren't sure if persisting was the answer. "There was some disquiet at the end of that game, there were people shouting: 'You're getting sacked in the morning.'"

While such sentiment may be difficult to swallow for many coaches, Parker said that Hürzeler told him in an interview soon after joining the club that he welcomed it when needed.

"He talked about wanting a fan relationship that had a two-way aspect. The club and him are really ambitious, so if the performances aren't up to scratch, we should be telling him that. And that's what happened on that day. I see the whole thing as being quite healthy."

Hürzeler never played at the top level. He represented Germany's youth teams and turned out for Bayern Munich's reserves but soon grew frustrated with second-team football. He then accepted a player-coach role at German fifth-tier side Pipinsried at the age of 23. From 2018, he was also an assistant coach for Germany's U20s.

He performed this alongside a job at an art dealership in the German state of Bavaria, where he moved with his family at the age of two having been born in the United States. After starting as an assistant coach at St. Pauli in 2020, he took over after head coach Timo Schultz was fired in late 2022. Since then, he hasn't looked back.

That unusual path to top-flight management and some innovative tactics at St. Pauli led to a perception in Germany that Hürzeler was a little aloof and something of a 'laptop manager' in the vein of former Bayern Munich and Germany boss, Julian Nagelsmann who had a similarly nondescript playing career. This, so the charge goes, meant Hürzeler wasn't able to forge the relationships and togetherness needed to make a team more than the sum of its parts.

That was rarely what was reported by his players and staff at St. Pauli, nor is it Hürzeler's belief. "I want to be myself, I don't want to play a role, and my age definitely helps regarding understanding the players," he said.

"I always say I speak their language and I understand their thoughts, because it wasn't that long ago when I played."

His antics on the sideline also earned him a reputation as a bit of a hothead. Hürzeler was booked seven times during St. Pauli's promotion push and since joining Brighton, the German has been booked nine times and been sent off once. When asked about this, he said: "Emotions are part of the game."

Parker said this authenticity has also been reflected in his relationship with Brighton and Hove, on the south coast of England.

"For most Brighton fans he comes across as quite a quirky, interesting, left-field figure. The mantra he set out when he first arrived was quite counter-culturalist, to challenge the establishment, and that fits well here," Parker said.

"You will see him walking along on the seafront, going up for coffees around town, and he travels back and forth on an ebike, not in a chauffer-driven car as a lot of managers might. He's also hosted fan events in pubs, which I believe he paid for. So I'd say he's very approachable."

But Hürzeler isn't the only 30-something German beloved in Brighton.

Pascal Gross, who rejoined the club from Borussia Dortmund in January, is also a firm favorite. The midfielder, who retired from Germany duty after the World Cup earlier this year, has scored three and made four in the club's opening seven league games. The 35-year-old's connection with Hürzeler is also key, with Groß admitting he stayed in touch with Hürzeler even before he resigned. The return is proving to look a great decision for both sides.

"I was here for seven years, got married here and both my kids were born in England. The most important milestones in my life happened here. I missed my friends and the feeling of being deeply connected to the club."

The feeling is mutual, said Parker. "Pascal Gross is everybody's favorite player. He's Brighton's first best signing, from Ingolstadt, and second-best signing, from Dortmund. He's a sensational player, and it's probably true to say there is a lot of warmth towards German football and Germany because of these hugely important characters at the football club."

The Premier League club's success has been built on a smart coach and player recruitment strategy guided by local owner, Tony Bloom. Part of the model is that those who shine brightest will often be snatched by the bigger fish.

"I think he's said he's a supporter of Bayern Munich, and he uses them as an example of the standards he wants," said Parker of Hürzeler. "I can see that he could be a good fit in a couple of years time. He won't go to a Liverpool or a Chelsea, I think there's a strong pull to Bayern in particular."

Bayern's current boss, Vincent Kompany, is in little danger at the moment, though Bayern coaches are only ever a few losses from crisis. For the meantime, Hürzeler is also happy where he is, having extended his contract to 2029. Again, the feeling is mutual.

Next up in the Premier League is a trip to Liverpool, where Jürgen Klopp became the first German coach to make a real mark on the Premier League. But before that, Hürzeler's team have an assignment in the Europa Conference League, a competition Brighton are among the favorites to win. Parker hopes a first major trophy is in sight.

"If he can be the person that wins us that first trophy, then he will go down as the greatest."

#830. Russell Brand Found Guilty of Rape, 3 Counts of Sexual Assault

Russell Brand has been convicted of rape and multiple counts of sexual assault over a year after his legal battle began in London.

Russell Brand’s legal battle has reached a conclusion.

On Nov. 5, a London court found the 51-year-old was convicted on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

After deliberating for over eight hours, according to multiple outlets, the jury found Brand guilty of raping a fan in 2009 after meeting at one of his shows in London, of groping an MTV worker in 2004, kissing and groping another woman at her workplace in 2009 and of sexually assaulting another woman in 2009.

Brand—who had pleaded not guilty to all charges—was cleared of two separate counts of rape and one count of indecent assault.

The presiding judge Joel Bennathan, according to The New York Times, said he would sentence the Forgetting Sarah Marshall actor to “significant custodial time,” while also denying him bail.

British sentencing guidelines for rape, per the outlet, carry a maximum sentence of life in prison, while the average prison term for such a conviction is four to 19 years.

Brand’s legal battle began in April 2025, when he was charged with one count of rape, one count of oral rape, two counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault by the London Metropolitan Police. The events in question allegedly occurred between 1999 and 2009.

In December 2025, the actor was also charged with one additional count of rape and one more sexual assault charge, the London Metropolitan Police confirmed in a press release.

At the time, Brand—father to three with wife Laura Brand—shared a video to social media urging viewers “to understand the truth of my situation and scenario,” though he didn’t address the allegations directly.

“I pray Lord, anyone that I’ve harmed or hurt in my years of mindlessness and sin would be healed, Lord,” he said in the clip. “And I pray, Lord, for the absolute truth of who I am to be abundantly revealed.”

Despite the convictions, however, Brand’s legal journey may not be done.

According to the New York Times, citing an emailed statement following the verdicts, a spokeswoman for the Metropolitan Police said police had questioned Brand about two additional accusations of rape, submitting the files to prosecutors.

During the trial, per the outlet, Brand did not deny that some of the encounters had occurred, though he claimed every act had been consensual.

He reportedly told jurors, per the NYT, that while he “misused” his fame to obtain sexual encounters, he had always obtained consent, saying doing so had been “fundamental, essential, necessary.”

E! News has reached out to Brand’s legal team for comment but has not yet heard back.

Following Brand’s conviction, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy released a statement praising the verdict.

“As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement,” Furphy said, per CNN. “I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be.”

#829. Beverly Hills, 90210 Actress Kimmarie Johnson Dead at 50

Kimmarie Johnson, who starred in Beverly Hills 90210 and Dude, Where’s My Car? has died after suffering heart issues, her niece told TMZ. She was 50.

The sun has set too soon on the life of another beloved Beverly Hills, 90210 star.

Kimmarie Johnson, who portrayed Judy in multiple episodes of the teen drama, died following a “heart event,” her niece Rhonda Scott told TMZ Nov. 5. She was 50.

Johnson, per TMZ, experienced the medical emergency on Oct. 27 at her home in Los Angeles before being rushed to Cedars-Sinai Hospital. There, she was diagnosed with a “heart aneurysm condition,” per the outlet. She died Nov. 4 after her heart stopped beating.

After a small role in Let’s Talk About Sex, Johnson made her debut on Beverly Hills, 90210 in 1998, working alongside the likes of Jennie Garth, Tori Spelling and Brian Austin Green.

She later went on to have small roles in projects such as Dude, Where’s My Car? alongside Austin Kutcher and Jennifer Garner in 2000, in addition to other film roles through 2017, when she made her last on-screen appearance as Rebekah in Tucker’s War.

Aside from her acting career, Johnson founded her own skincare consulting company, Skin Glow, in 2011 and modeled for print campaigns and runway shows. In 1993, she won the Miss Pennsylvania USA Beauty Pageant and went on to be a finalist in the Miss USA competition.

Born in Pittsburgh, Johnson graduated from Wilkinsburg High School in 1985. She went on to study at California University in Pennsylvania, before moving to New York City and then Los Angeles to pursue. a career in modeling.

Johnson is survived by her niece, as well as her son Cameron Nino, who was born in 2003.

Johnson’s passing comes after Beverly Hills, 90210 has had a difficult few years of loss, with Shannen Doherty dying in 2024 following a yearslong battle with breast cancer and David Gail dying the same year from cardiac arrest.

Following Doherty’s death, Garth—who acknowledged she and Doherty were “pitted against each other” on Beverly Hills—called her “courageous, passionate, determined and very loving and generous.”

“Our connection was real and honest,” Garth wrote in a tribute at the time. “I will miss her and will always honor her deeply in my heart and in my memories.”

To revisit memories from Beverly Hills, keep reading…

Created by Darren Star, the show was originally called Class of Beverly Hills, and at one point, Star, who based the show loosely on his own high school experience in Potomac, Md., used the working title Potomac 20854 before its now-iconic title was settled on.

While Beverly Hills, 90210 would go on to become one of the most popular TV shows of the '90s and be largely responsible for launching the teen soap genre, the Fox show was a dud when it first debuted in 1990, ranking No. 118 in the ratings (going up against NBC's Cheers didn't help).

But after the season one finale, featuring Brenda and Dylan's first time, started gaining buzz, Fox smartly ordered new episodes for the summer, providing some much-needed teen angst and drama in what used to be the TV off-season.

"We filmed all of our risqué summer episodes at the beach and aired those at the time when the other shows were in reruns," Jennie Garth told the New York Times. "So we caught a huge teen audience, kids that were home from school. And then it just went crazy."

From there, 90210 went from low-rated guilty pleasure to cultural phenomenon and the mostly unknown stars became some of the most famous people in the world.

"In just a matter of weeks, we went from being just another generic ensemble cast of any old prime-time drama to being…superstars," Garth wrote in her memoir. "I don't think any of us were prepared for the stardom that was thrust upon us in this way."

Before being cast as one of TV's ultimate heartthrobs, Luke Perry was working construction as a way to pay his bills between auditions—including for the role of Steve Sanders, which ultimately went to Ian Ziering.

But when producers realized they were lacking a brooding bad boy, Perry, then 27, got the call. "When Luke walked into the audition, it was like 'Wow, that's the person,'" Star gushed to Rolling Stone. "He seems exactly like James Dean to me, but it isn't a conscious imitation—he's really being himself."

Dylan McKay was initially only going to appear in a few episodes, but it was clear from the moment he drove up in that black Porsche 356 Speedster that a star was born—though Spelling had to fight to make Perry a series regular. (Imagine their reaction when they learned 20 people were injured after a riot broke out at a mall during one of Perry's appearances when 10,000 fans showed up?)

Perry remained on the show until 1995, leaving for three years to pursue other opportunities before returning in 1998, and remained on until the end, often credited as a special guest star.

In March 2019, Perry died at the age of 52 after suffering a stroke. He was starring on Riverdale, the latest teen soap that can credit the original 90210 for leading the way, playing the father of Archie (KJ Apa), the show's brooding lead. While he wasn't set to appear on Fox's BH90210 revival that year, the show paid tribute to the beloved star in its premiere.

Fearful of nepotism, executive producer Aaron Spelling's daughter Tori Spelling auditioned under a fake name, Tori Mitchell (inspired by a character Heather Locklear played in a TV movie her dad produced), reading for the roles of Kelly and Andrea before landing the role of Donna Martin.

"I heard about the show from my agent. She said, 'Your dad is doing it.' I was like, 'I haven't heard anything about it,'" Spelling told EW. "I popped into his briefcase when he got home, and I was like, cool. I really wanted to play Andrea. I went in under a different name, then I got the part of Donna—which I'm sure had something to do with my dad."

Donna ended up the cener of many an iconic moment, including the infamous "Donna Martin graduates!" chant when getting drunk on prom night got her banned from the graduation ceremony. In his memoir, Jason Priestley revealed a prank he pulled on that day of filming: Knowing they were going to reloop the dialogue anyway, Priestley got the group of extras to chant "Donna Martin masturbates!" instead, finding the opportunity "pretty irresistible."

Shannen Doherty, previously known for the pitch-black high school comedy Heathers, was named the cast's Biggest Diva upon graduation from West Beverly, and Brenda Walsh only stayed through one season of 90210's college years.

"Her lateness was appalling, and she had a callous attitude and an indifference," former executive producer Charles Rosin told EW in 2000. Aaron Spelling added, "It wasn't like she ruined the show or anything. It just upset the cast members tremendously."

Doherty admitted, "There was definitely a time that I did not want to be there. I was unhappy."

The final straw for producers was rumored to be Doherty's decision to cut her hair in the middle of filming the season four finale in 1994, which saw Brenda deciding to move to London to pursue acting.

But later Spelling admitted going to her father to expedite Doherty's firing.

"I felt like I was a part of something, a movement, that cost someone their livelihood," an emotional Spelling said during a 2015 special. "Was she a horrible person? No. She was one of the best friends I ever had."

After Doherty's death at 53 in July 2024 following a years-long battle with breast cancer, all of her former costars paid tribute. Priestley called her a "force of nature," while Spelling remembered her as "a rebel in an era when most women didn’t feel comfortable being strong."

After Doherty's dramatic exit, the pressure was on to find her replacement.

"We obviously had an exhaustive search to replace her," executive producer Larry Mollin told TeenDramaW--re in 2010. "We looked at many people."

Alicia Silverstone, Alyssa Milano and Drew Barrymore were all reportedly in contention, but 90210 went with Saved By the Bell star Tiffani Amber-Thiessen, whose scheming Valerie Malone was the opposite of cheery Kelly Kapowski.

"We wanted a baaad girl. There was really an edge with Tiffani because she was so sexual," producer Rosin told EW. "In her first episode, she [smoked] some pot. We were making a statement there." (In her first scene, she memorably rolls a joint with one hand, though a stunt double was needed.)

Viewers responded immediately to the character, but there was one cast member who didn't love Thiessen: Brian Austin Green, her real-life boyfriend at the time.

"When we cast her, Brian was so upset! Oh my god, he felt betrayed!" Mollin recalled. "We were totally shocked and had no idea. But, then, of course, we realized why: because other people would be kissing...his girlfriend!"

Fact: If you assemble a cast of young, attractive, available people and have them work together for an extended period of time, they will hook up.

"Various combinations of people slept with each other over the years," Priestley shared in his memoir, undoubtedly filling fans with righteous joy that their suspicions were right all these years later. Priestley went on to say his "full-fledged adult relationship" was with Christine Elise (aka Emily Valentine), whom he dated for five years.

During a test on Celebrity Lie Detector, Spelling said she had a quick summer fling with Priestley, dated Green (saying she was "always in love" with her onscreen beau), and once kissed Perry. (Priestley's response? "I'm not getting into this... It's nobody's business... Either way...," he tweeted.)

After dating Thiessen for several years, Green started seeing Vanessa Marcil, who played one of David's non-Donna love interests, Gina Kincaid. They split up in 2003 and share now grown son Kassius.

If viewers thought the rivalry between Brenda and Kelly was intense, it was nothing compared to the behind-the-scenes feuding between Doherty and Garth, with Spelling often attempting (and failing) to play peacemaker.

"I don't know why it is, but there is a universal truth that when you put three teenage girls together, some serious s--t is going to go down," Garth wrote in her 2013 memoir, "even if it meant sounding like a complete and utter b---h. Poor Tori, the youngest of the three of us was, inevitably, often caught in the middle and she was always trying to smooth things over, trying to get Shan and me off each other's backs and get along, but her efforts usually failed."

Things got so heated that the two stars once came very close to throwing punches (with some accounts saying fists actually did fly), with Garth revealing the cause of the blowup (which the male cast members had to step in to de-escalate): Doherty pulled up Garth's skirt while filming a scene. Garth, describing the two of them as "gasoline and a match," wrote, "I did snap and I yelled at her, something to the effect of, 'Come on, b---h! We're talking this outside!'"

Fortunately, Doherty and Garth ultimately reconciled.

"Our connection was real and honest," Garth wrote on Instagram after Doherty's death. "We were so often pitted against each other but none of that reflected the truth of our real relationship which was one built on mutual respect and admiration."

It might be hard to believe, but back in the early '90s, 16-year-old Brenda losing her virginity to Dylan at the spring dance was a big effin' deal. And the biggest outcry came from scandalized local affiliates (or the people who wrote in to them to complain) who were upset that Brenda's first time was...perfectly fine!

"I was strongly advised to write a show that would address the consequences of that sexual experience," Star revealed to The New York Times. "So the first episode of the second season Brenda broke up with Dylan because their relationship had gotten too mature."

While Kelly Taylor was battling cults, cocaine use, love triangles and amnesia onscreen, Garth was privately struggling with anxiety from the age of 19, as she revealed in her memoir.

"I felt comfortable—almost comforted—by all of the workers buzzing around me during the day, but after hours, I'd find myself getting anxious when strangers approached me," she wrote. "And so simple tasks, like going to the grocery store, or the mall, or to get gas, became overwhelming exercises in having to be ‘on' when my natural inclination was to shut down and not interact with anyone. I…began to suffer a level of anxiety that as, at times, nearly paralyzing. When the panic attacks started to kick in, I became even more withdrawn."

She revealed at one point she had "stopped going to the movies or clothes shopping or doing any of the other things normal young people do," waiting until well after dark to step out of her home. "I wouldn't say that I ever stepped over the line into full-blown agoraphobia, but I would say I definitely came close."

While Ziering mostly avoided any and all drama on set, he revealed he had an emotional breakdown in season four after a storyline of Steve's was cut.

"There was an episode where Steve was accused of rape," he told HuffPost Live in 2015. "But, they edited out so much powerful stuff. That was like the first time I really got some great words to say and I work-shopped them and I studied. I brought game, and it never even made it through the edit."

Feeling "betrayed" by the producers' decision not to air the scenes without letting him know first, Ziering lost his cool.

"I tore the dressing rooms apart," he revealed. "We all work so hard for our characters and to not even get a heads up...I'm not a volatile person, I have a very long fuse, but after working so hard on this particular episode, I just didn't feel like they were with me on this one."

Jason Priestley's Partying and Parting Ways

After becoming a heartthrob as ultimate nice guy Brandon, Priestley was desperate to shed the goody-two-shoes image in real life, so he indulged in some hard partying "to prove that I was nothing like the sanctimonious Brandon Walsh," he wrote in his memoir. (During a 2014 Watch What Happens Live! appearance, Garth said he partied the hardest out of all the cast members.)

"When you're young like that, you feel like a hamster on a wheel. All you're doing is spinning that wheel and your world," he told The Hollywood Reporter. "You have a bunch of people telling you how great you are, so it's really easy to just start believing it after a while."

Priestley ended up changing his ways (thanks in large part to his relationship with costar Elise), going on to become a producer on the show and directing episodes, which is why Brandon's unceremonious exit in season nine hurt his feelings at the time.

"I did the first scene of the morning—literally with this actor who was brought in to replace me—and that was it. I hugged the crew, picked up my box of stuff, went to my car and drove away," he told the Guardian. "There was no party, no nothing. I felt like I'd wasted nine years of my life."

He returned in a video message—Brandon's well-wishes for Donna and David when they tied the knot—for the series finale in 2000.

After initially auditioning for Brenda, believing that being a twin IRL would give her an edge, Gabrielle Carteris landed the role of Andrea—after the 29-year-old lied about her age to snag the part of the academically minded 16-year-old. (Fun fact: Teen Witch star Robyn Lively, then Priestley's girlfriend, turned down the role of Andrea first.)

"I actually talked to a lawyer about how could I sign these contracts and lie about my age and still be able to do the show. Is it OK?" she told Access Hollywood. "[The lawyer said] ‘Yes it is, as long as you just say you're over 21.'"

A main cast member for the first five seasons, producers reluctantly worked Carteris' real-life pregnancy into the show, making Andrea pregnant and marrying her off to the baby's father, her boyfriend Jesse Vasquez (Mark Espinoza). But by the end of the fifth season, the producers felt Andrea's time in America's most famous zip code had run its course and sent her off to Yale with her young family.

"It didn't really add to us. It took away a lot of the fun, to have to be in this grown-up stuff," Mollin said. "We eventually just didn't think it was going to work."

Two Oscar wins later, Hilary Swank is still not over being fired from Beverly Hills, 90210 back in the day.

After playing single mom Carly Reynolds for 13 episodes in season eight, Swank was unexpectedly fired despite having signed a two-year contract, leaving her "devastated" after learning fans didn't love her character paired with Steve Sanders.

"They were like, 'Look, it's not working,'" Swank said on Conan of the conversation she had with producers. "And I couldn't move. I was like, 'What's not working? Me? Am I bad? I'm not working because I'm bad?'"

But when one door closes, another opens, and soon after her firing Swank landed her (first) Oscar-winning role in 1999's Boys Don't Cry.

#828. FA and WSL launch major study into ACL injuries in women's football

Leah Williamson, Beth Mead and Mary Fowler have all experienced ACL injuries

The Football Association and WSL Football have launched a major research project to better understand why anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries occur in women's football and identify ways to reduce them.

Funded by the FA, the PhD study with Imperial College London and sports knee surgeon Simon Ball will be led by researcher Hanna Lehtovirta and involve clubs across the Women's Super League and WSL2.

ACL injuries are among the most serious issues facing the women's game, often keeping players out for months.

Research suggests female footballers are two to six times more likely to suffer the injury than their male counterparts.

Vivianne Miedema, Beth Mead, Leah Williamson and Sam Kerr are among the players to have suffered the injury over recent years.

While previous studies have highlighted potential risk factors including anatomical, hormonal, biomechanical and environmental influences, researchers say less is known about how those factors interact in the day-to-day experience of elite football.

The study aims to provide one of the most comprehensive examinations of ACL injuries in women's football by combining scientific data with the experiences of players and staff.

Players from every WSL and WSL2 club will be invited to take part, alongside medical, performance and coaching staff.

The research will be conducted in two phases.

The first will use player surveys to gather data on injury history, training and match load, and hormonal, nutritional and psychological factors.

Data from players who have suffered ACL injuries since 2018-19 will be compared with those who have not.

The second phase will involve interviews with players and staff to explore perceptions of ACL injuries and current approaches to training and prevention.

Researchers hope the findings will help shape future injury prevention, rehabilitation and player welfare strategies in the women's game.

In April 2025, Fifa announced they were also funding research into whether hormonal fluctuations during menstrual cycles could be contributing to the rise in ACL injuries in women's football.

#827. Japan FA’s Kozo Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency

Tashima says he brings ‘honest, sound, upright attitude’

He is understood to have acted with the blessing of Uefa

The Japan Football Association’s honorary president, Kozo Tashima, has announced his intention to stand against Gianni Infantino in March’s Fifa presidential election.

Tashima is the second challenger to declare in advance of the 18 November deadline after the former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega, although it remains unclear whether Vega has the backing of five of Fifa’s 211 member associations, which is required to take a place on the ballot in Rabat.

The widely respected Tashima will have no problem in securing the nominations and is understood to have acted with the blessing of Uefa, which has led the opposition to Infantino after his failed attempt to sell off a 20% stake in Fifa’s commercial rights this summer. The former Japan international has many allies in Europe and had talks with Uefa officials at last month’s Asian Football Confederation (AFC) congress in Tokyo.

“I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association,” Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. “It’s not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What Fifa needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order ‌to make this appeal to the world.”

Tashima could split the AFC vote and is certain to pick up votes from Europe and Concacaf, although other candidates could emerge.

#826. Off Campus Season 2 Premiere Date Revealed

Off Campus season two is skating to screens this spring with Stephen Kalyn's Dean Di Laurentis and Mika Abdalla's Allie Hayes romance taking center ice. Keep reading for everything to know.

Off Campus is ready to bring the heat back to Briar University's ice.

After all, the hockey romance is returning with more games, love and betrayal in its highly anticipated second season on April 28, the series confirmed on social media.

Stephen Kalyn, who plays hockey star Dean Di Laurentis, answered a knock at the door, asking the camera in the Nov. 5 Instagram video, "What? Did you miss us?" Mika Abdalla, who is returning as theater student Allie Hayes, added, "Dean and Allie are officially back for season two," before the door closed with the show's premiere date on the sign.

The second installment kicks off after an explosive season one finale, which ended when a love triangle between Allie, Dean, and fellow hockey player Hunter Davenport (Charlie Evans) came to a head in the form of a blowout fight.

The charged encounter set the stage for friends-with-benefits Dean and Allie—the best friend of Hannah Wells (Ella Bright), last season's leading lady opposite Garrett Graham (Belmont Cameli)—to step into center ice, with their game-winning romance acting as the main storyline for season two.

Meanwhile, John Logan (Antoni Cipriano) will be skating through the early chapters of his own love story with Grace Ivers (India Fowler).

"We are so excited to continue Allie and Dean's story as our primary romance of season 2 after kickstarting their romance in season 1," showrunner Louisa Levy announced in a May statement. "But if you fell in love with Hannah and Garrett, don't worry—they will still be an integral part of our robust ensemble."

Though Dean and Allie's love story is part of Elle Kennedy's third novel The Score—Logan and Grace are the leads of the second, The Mistake—Levy noted the momentum of the first season led to the change-up.

"I wanted viewers to know who they were going to be tuning in for next," she told Variety at the time. "Allie felt so organic, because she's Hannah's best friend and Dean is already there, and their love story in the book is a secret—so why not let it be a surprise, even to book fans, when we're going to launch it?"

"Some things had to work a little differently because of the timing and the way we platform them," she continued, "but I promise all the fan-favorite things are still intended and planned. There's still a lot of road with those two."

For instance, Hunter—whom Allie had a one-night stand with before seeing the animosity between him and Dean, which prompted the aforementioned brawl—was necessary as an antagonist in the Prime Video show.

"He also comes from the same world as Dean, which made his arrival feel organic," she explained. "We needed to throw a wrench into Dean and Allie's arrangement to elongate their story, and pulling from that universe felt right."

For Kennedy's part, the author is looking forward to seeing Logan and Grace's budding romance begin to play out.

"I did get to see the chemistry tests with Antonio and India, who is cast as Grace, and they are spectacular together," she told E! News ahead of the season one premiere. "That's what I'm probably most excited for."

"She rambles when she's nervous and she's just so random," she added of the new character. "I think people will really resonate with her because she is just awkward. There are moments where, in the book, I was writing it and I was cringing, I'm like, 'No, Grace, shut up!' I'm very excited to see that."

Meanwhile, his sister Casey Cartwright (Spencer Grammer) is a member of Beta Zeta and Cappie's ex-girlfriend. The series follows six chapters at CRU, where parties, drama and excitement ensue. Oh, and a lot of beer pong.

Lydia's twin brother James (Damian Hardung), in an attempt to ensure Ruby's silence, tries to bribe her with money and then with his body.

An unimpressed Ruby—a low-income student on scholarship at the tony prep school—declined both of the arrogant lacrosse stars' deals. But while the pair initially despises one another, it doesn't take long before that frustration turns into passion.

All that's left is for Ruby and James to navigate their budding feelings while grappling with the repercussions of their socioeconomic differences. Will love be enough for a happily ever after?

You really shouldn't wanna wait to take the metaphorical trip to Capeside for this six-season series centering Dawson Leery (James Van Der Beek) and his best friends Joey Potter (Katie Holmes) and Pacey Witter (Joshua Jackson).

The show begins with 15-year-old aspiring filmmaker Dawson and his BFF Joey, who is not-so-secretly in love with him, as they navigate adolescence with their friends in the fictional Massachusetts town. Along with exploring topics such as first love, teen pregnancy, racism, drugs and more, the series was a trailblazer in queer media.

"[The scene] gave millions of people a storyline that was reflective of their reality," Kaufman told Us Weekly in May 2020. "I'm so honored to have been a part of that."

#824. Fifa wants talks over restricting women’s Olympic football to under-23s

IOC open to dialogue and Fifa wants input from others

Fifa concerned about fixture congestion and workload

Fifa wants talks with the International Olympic Committee over restricting the Olympic women’s football tournament to under-23s owing to concerns over fixture congestion and the workload of senior players.

The eligibility criteria for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles has been set, with qualification tournaments having begun in some regions, so no change can be made until Brisbane 2032 at the earliest, but sources at both organisations have said that they are open to dialogue.

Although no formal proposal has been made, Fifa is understood to be interested in examining the matter in talks with the IOC and other key stakeholders, such as the players and leading member associations whose national sides routinely qualify for the Games.

A move to bring in age restrictions would dramatically alter the nature of the event and require careful analysis, consultation and consideration through Fifa and IOC processes.

Such a change would be controversial and could provoke a backlash from leading international players because the Olympics has long been regarded as one of the highlights of the women’s calendar, with Emma Hayes’s United States team securing gold in Paris two years ago. The Olympic title has been contested eight times and the US have won five.

Women’s football also has a major commercial appeal for the IOC, particularly in markets such as the US, Europe and Australia, so it may resist Fifa’s overtures.

Women’s football was introduced to the Olympics at Atlanta in 1996, and as an amateur sport at that time never had eligibility requirements, in contrast to the men’s game.

After admitting football to the Olympic programme in 1908 the IOC did not permit professionals to take part until 1984 owing to Fifa’s insistence on maintaining the primacy of the World Cup, as well as the demands on players from a congested calendar. Under pressure from Fifa the IOC introduced an under-23 age restriction in 1992, although three overage players have also been allowed in each squad since 1996.

The huge growth and professionalisation of the women’s game over the past decade has created increased fixture congestion, with the 2028 calendar the most bloated yet.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Fifa is to a large extent culpable for this because the world governing body has chosen to launch the Women’s Club World Cup in an Olympic year, with the US to stage the 16-team competition between 5 and 30 January, six months before the Games.

The Women’s Club World Cup will cause major disruption to the European club season, with Arsenal and Chelsea or Manchester City likely to be absent from domestic competition for up to a month if they reach the latter stages, missing four Women’s Super League matches and the FA Cup fourth round. The importance of the sport to the IOC is shown by the fact that the women’s football tournament will be bigger than the men’s for the first time in LA, featuring 16 teams to 12, in a reversal of the numbers at Paris 2024.

#823. Travis Kelce Teases Holiday Plans After Taylor Swift Wedding

Travis Kelce couldn’t hold back his excitement as he prepares for his first holiday season with his now-wife Taylor Swift.

Travis Kelce is ready to leave the Christmas lights up until at least January.

This is his and Taylor Swift’s place, and they’re making the rules as they head into the holiday season hot off the heels of their July nuptials.

“I’m excited for my first holiday as a married man,” Kelce told WWD Nov. 5 while in conversation about his new campaign with Tommy Hilfiger. “I love all the old traditions and can’t wait to start some new ones.”

And as soon as the Christmas lights start to glisten, the Kansas City Chiefs tight end will be simply having a wonderful Christmastime.

As he put it, “I start celebrating as that tree goes up.”

But that begs the question, did he ever stop celebrating since he said, “I do,” in New York City?

After all, the 37-year-old previously called his and Swift’s wedding “the best night of my life.”

“Marrying Taylor was more than I could have ever dreamed it to be,” he added during his September convo with ESPN’s Chris Berman, “because of all the people that showed up, and the amount of, you know, love that was in the air."

In fact, Kelce and Swift had to make their way through a crowd of nearly 1,000 well-wishers who descended on New York’s Madison Square Garden to witness the next chapter in the pair’s love story.

“Me and Taylor are so thankful for everybody that showed up,” Kelce said during the Sept. 2 episode of his New Heights podcast with brother Jason Kelce. “From the vows to the seeing everyone to how much fun we had throughout the entire evening, and hearing that being relayed through everyone’s stories of that night—it was just so magical man, I wish it could have lasted longer than it did."

“It was so cool to see everyone from my childhood not only mesh with Taylor, but [the people] from her childhood and her family and friends," he explained, "and people that she works with to people that we’ve encountered over the course of our career and who we just admire as people and have become good friends with now."

43 players and eight members of staff received red cards after the brawl, as well as two board members

A world record of 53 red cards were shown during a chaotic under-20s game in Brazil.

Uberlandia goalkeeping coach Paulo Sergio Dias Dos Santos ran on to the pitch to confront him, sparking clashes and the subsequent dismissals, with three players having already been sent off earlier.

"Therefore, owing to all the turmoil and the lack of security, I declared the match ended."

#821. Cape Verde captain Ryan Mendes cleared of rape allegation as woman charged with false statement

New Zealand police dismiss claim of sexual assault at Auckland hotel

Incident alleged to have occurred after football friendly in March

New Zealand police have dismissed a rape allegation against Cape Verde football captain Ryan Mendes and have charged the accuser with making a false statement.

Detective inspector Scott Beard said Friday the claim that a sexual assault occurred at a central Auckland hotel in March had not been substantiated.

A 40-year-old woman has been charged under New Zealand’s Crimes Act with making a false statement. She is expected to appear in court next week.

“A decision to prosecute in these circumstances is not taken lightly and follows months of investigative work by our Adult Sexual Assault Team,” Beard said.

The incident was alleged to have occurred hours after Cape Verde played Chile in a friendly match in Auckland, won 4-2 by Chile.

Mendes’ lawyer, Karl Trotter, said the allegation resulted in his client facing intense international media speculation.

Cape Verde qualified for the 2026 World Cup and the subject of the alleged assault arose at almost every media conference Mendes attended.

“Mr Mendes was thrilled to finally be able to get this behind him and he regards it as a complete vindication,” Karl Trotter told the New Zealand Herald newspaper.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“It is to be hoped that this recent turn of events, clearing Mr Mendes of the allegation of rape, attracts the same level of media attention as the original reporting.”

The 36-year-old Mendes is Cape Verde’s most capped player, having made 103 appearances since his debut in 2010. He currently plays for RS Berkane in Morocco.

#820. US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors

As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.

The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult.

On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.

Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.

Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it.

Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives.

The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan.

The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies.

Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days.

In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days.

For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz. But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences.

A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability.

It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days.

The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran.

Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay.

Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries.

Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade.

"A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW.

Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport.

That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges.

For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit.

Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging.

If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived.

"Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it."

The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation.

Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited.

Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels.

Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks.

"Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said.

That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices.

Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel.

Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight.

#819. Scott Parker’s dramatic West Ham return leaves him struggling for words

The former midfielder with impressive managerial promotion record began with a thrilling comeback in draw at Cardiff

Three days in and Scott Parker has already lost his voice. West Ham’s head coach arrived on Tuesday, watched his side fight back from 3-0 down to draw with Cardiff on Wednesday and was struggling to make himself heard when he met the media on Thursday afternoon.

“It’s like in the summer holidays,” Parker said. “You put the flip-flops on for five weeks, then you come back home and you get your shoes on. You’re in a minute, you’ve got a blister on the back of your heel. It’s the same with a throat. I’ve not shouted for a little while. All of a sudden there’s shouting and it’s a bit croaky.”

Parker is back in the thick of it. Out of work after leaving Burnley in the wake of relegation from the Premier League last April, he cut short his break from management when West Ham parted company with Nuno Espírito Santo. Nuno was sacked early on Tuesday and replaced by Parker, who is intent on leading West Ham out of the Championship at the first time of asking.

It will not be easy. West Ham occupy the final playoff spot after three games without a win and displayed their inconsistencies against Cardiff. They made another slow start, conceding three during the first half, but roared back after a triple half-time change from Parker. Jarrod Bowen was inspired. But Parker needs complete performances if West Ham are to win automatic promotion.

“The Championship’s a tough league,” he said. “It doesn’t matter what name you have on a bit of paper. You have to have a level of humility of what this league needs. That’s a challenge when you come out of the Premier League.”

Parker argued that talent was not enough. Burnley were stingy when they won promotion. Parker has to sort out West Ham’s defence. “Of course we want to play a certain brand,” the 46-year-old said. “But I think it’s just a non-negotiable in terms of a committed team.”

Connections need to be rebuilt with disillusioned supporters. Parker was an all-action midfielder who loved his four years at West Ham as a player. He has added Mark Noble to his backroom staff. Noble has held the role of West Ham’s sporting director since retiring in 2022 but Parker confirmed the former club captain would have a role as an assistant coach. “He’s going to be coaching with me and be that sounding board,” Parker said.

Noble will be able to get Parker up to speed on his squad. West Ham need improvement at the back, better balance in midfield and more bite up front. Nils Koppen, the director of recruitment, could be busy in January. Parker wants to give everyone a clean slate, though. Soungoutou Magassa and Edson Álvarez will have opportunities. Even Maxwel Cornet travelled with the squad to Cardiff.

Parker did not focus during negotiations with Karim Virani, West Ham’s interim CEO, and Daniel Kretinsky, the club’s largest shareholder, on whether funds would be available for signings. One step at a time.

West Ham are in transition. David Sullivan still owns a 40% stake but is no longer on the board. Kretinsky’s power has grown, although the Czech billionaire is yet to say much in public. Parker has heard more from Kretinsky than most people.

“I found a man that was hugely passionate,” Parker said. “I instantly felt that, along with Karim, along with Nils. These were three people who know where they want the club to go.”

The target is a return to the top flight. Parker has won promotion with Bournemouth, Burnley and Fulham but his record at keeping teams up is less impressive. He has been dismissed a little unfairly as nothing more than a promotion specialist.

“In a short space of a coaching career I’ve had some huge success,” Parker said. “I’ve had some blips in terms of two full seasons in the Premier League. All I know is that I’m fully committed.”

That mindset convinced Kretinsky, Virani and Koppen to pick Parker. They wanted his knowledge of the club and record at this level.

West Ham are eighth before visiting Blackburn Rovers on Saturday. They are taking 7,000 fans to Ewood Park and Parker knows there can be no more complacency.

#818. English female coach Kaminski reaping rewards in Norway

Laura Kaminski guided Crystal Palace to the WSL 2 title in 2024

When English manager Laura Kaminski was approached to become the head coach of Norwegian club SK Brann in January, she could not turn it down.

She jumped at the opportunity to move abroad and develop her coaching skills and is even competing for a place in the Europa Cup quarter-finals next Wednesday.

It was a decision that paid off as 10 months later, she is celebrating a Norwegian league and cup double after a dream debut season.

"My time in the city [of Bergen] has been brilliant," the 38-year-old told BBC Sport.

"I can't go to the supermarket at the minute because so many people are stopping me to wish me congratulations, which is so nice.

"I'm over the moon and it was nice to get the title done before the last game so we can relax. I thought it was going to go right to the wire.

"It's been a competitive year. I've enjoyed every minute. We had a great night with all our fans, who were waiting for us to return from Oslo."

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Kaminski on the challenges for English coaches in WSL

Kaminski described it as a "hectic" year as she moved from London to Norway and away from her family to take on the Brann job.

The Englishwoman had spent over a year at Crystal Palace, where she led them to promotion to the Women's Super League in 2024.

She was sacked in February 2025 after a tough WSL season as Palace struggled to compete with better financially-backed clubs.

However, she is regarded as one of the country's brightest female managers and has added to her CV with her experiences in Norway.

"I've learned a lot. It's been chaotic - I counted that I have taken 65 flights in 11 months - so it's been exhausting, but what an experience!" added Kaminski.

"To go all the way up to the Arctic Circle and play away [games] in freezing cold conditions with horizontal snow, to beautiful days in Bergen.

"Palace was totally different to Brann. I'm at a club that expects to win the Toppserien [the Norwegian top-flight] as they believe they have invested the most.

"That's been a real challenge. The WSL is dominated by the favourites in the pack so it wasn't always the expectation to get three points against big teams [at Palace]."

Kaminski admits being away from loved ones is "hard" and she has had to be prepared to "make sacrifices" but Brann's trophy success makes it worth it.

She has also picked up new ideas for her coaching philosophy having experienced the high-risk, attack-minded football in Norway.

"Norwegian teams are almost guaranteed to concede every game because they play such attacking football with no fear, and a relentlessness to press," she added.

"That is a bit different to what I was used to. When I watched the tactical displays when I first came in, I was a little bit alarmed at what people were doing.

"But when you play against their sides, and against that [pressing], it is really difficult. It's given me a lot of fuel for the future.

"There are some really fit, fast and athletic players here. It's not a surprise that big, big clubs are coming in for them."

Laura Kaminski spent a year and a half at Crystal Palace

After a season in Norway, Kaminski believes she is a better coach.

She had spent over 15 years as an assistant manager at various clubs in the WSL 2 and WSL and a coaching role with England's under-19s before joining Palace.

But having added European experience to her CV, Kaminski hopes it will open the door to more opportunities in the future.

"I'd like to think I've got a well-rounded skillset to be able to manage at the top level. Right now, my focus is on Brann and a new chapter," said Kaminski.

"There's only two levels in England that are professional. I definitely wanted to get European exposure, which I was never going to get in England.

"At the time, I was in discussions with a few clubs but it was things that I'd done before, or the project wasn't matching.

"I knew that when I came to Brann, I was going to coach top-level players. I wanted to be at the top of the competition and I was desperate to win a trophy."

Kaminski has urged other female coaches in England to go abroad and gain experience as she believes opportunities are too few in the WSL.

A study from UK Coaching in October showed there has been a 6% decline in the overall number of female coaches in recent years.

There are currently three English female coaches in the WSL - Jo Potter at Crystal Palace, Amy Merricks at Birmingham City and Karen Hills at Charlton Athletic - and they all came up with promoted clubs this summer.

But Kaminski says she is "concerned" about where they might go next and hopes more opportunities in English men's football will open up soon.

"I ended up leaving the country to go and get what I thought I deserved and had earned the right to work in, in terms of the level," said Kaminski.

"There's more than one female out there that's capable [of working in men's football]. I don't think it's out of reach. I would always, certainly, be open to it.

"At the moment, for me, there's not enough consideration even for that opportunity to be given to female managers who are more than capable.

"I think the foundations are there for females to take the plunge but is the world of football ready? I'm unsure."

#817. Cristiano Ronaldo merely the latest example of a great player who couldn’t let go | Jonathan Wilson

There is no doubt his international career was an incredible one, but it would have been greater still if he had not lingered on the stage so long

Nothing, perhaps, is quite so difficult for an elite sportsperson as timing their exit. It’s not easy for any person in any job to weigh the hope of having more to give with the desire not to linger beyond their usefulness, but it’s perhaps particularly hard for top athletes because unrealistic self-confidence is so essential to their success. It takes an almost unhealthy level of self-belief for anybody to make the sacrifices to get to the top, to dedicate themselves to such a precarious vocation, to overcome all the setbacks and injuries and failures. How can someone – whose whole life has been spent assuring themselves there are no odds they cannot overcome – accept that is it, that the time has come to say goodbye?

The news that Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international football brings with it, inevitably, a sadness. Sadness we will no longer see him skipping past a defender, or burying a neck-thrusting header, and sadness in that the end of the career of any great is a reminder of mortality; all things in time must pass. But there is also a sadness he timed his departure so badly. For at least three tournaments, there has been a sense of Ronaldo holding Portugal back.

At the 2022 World Cup, Fernando Santos belatedly took the decision to leave Ronaldo out for the last-16 tie against Switzerland. Portugal suddenly had a fluency and fluidity they had lacked for years and the player who had replaced Ronaldo, Gonçalo Ramos, scored a hat-trick. That seemed incontrovertible evidence the end was upon Ronaldo, or at least his role might become that of an impact substitute.

But even in the final minutes of that game, half the crowd were chanting for Ronaldo. Some, perhaps, were Portuguese fans but many were tourists. They didn’t care much about the result or who went through, they just wanted to see the famous man do the famous thing. Near the end, he scored a goal that was obviously offside. He knew it was offside, but he also knew what his public wanted. So he did the “Siuuuu …” celebration and was rewarded with the biggest cheer of the night. This was like seeing late-period Elvis in Las Vegas: it didn’t matter he was no longer the singer he had been, he was still Elvis. It’s just that Elvis wasn’t also carrying Portugal’s World Cup hopes on his rhinestoned shoulders.

When a player has such celebrity status, when he is still somehow the show no matter how sluggish his movements, making that decision on when to quit must become even harder. And Ronaldo, with his status as Portugal’s greatest soft-power export, also became a political issue. A cabinet minister publicly said he couldn’t be dropped because of how much revenue he generated and what he meant for Portugal’s brand. Portugal is not a country replete with global superstars.

Portuguese Football Federation "Every drop of sweat, every decisive goal, and every captain’s arm-band he wore with honour on the field reflected his unconditional love ⁠for our jersey. His dedication ⁠and his legacy ​transcend the four lines of the field. Ronaldo has raised Portugal’s profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for ⁠many of us, he is the greatest player of all time! …"

Al-Nassr (Ronaldo's current club) "It’s not just a chapter – it’s history you’ve shaped. You’re an icon to the entire world, not ⁠just Portugal. Portugal is in your heart, and you are in the hearts of the world. A page ​has turned, but there is still history left ‌for us to write together at ‌your home, Al-Nassr."

Manchester United (one of Ronaldo's former clubs) "Congratulations on an incredible international career."

Bruno Fernandes (Portugal and Manchester United) "Thank ‌you for the inspiration. It was a privilege to be able to share great moments with our national team alongside my childhood idol."

Diogo Dalot (Portugal and Manchester United) "They don’t know that dreams are a constant in life … Portugal’s history tells us that we are a people who have never accepted limits, unafraid of uncharted seas or weathering storms. We were and are shaped by achievements, sacrifices, tears, and sweat … ‌By dreams that seem impossible – until someone has the courage to make them a reality. You did it. You made us believe, dream, and achieve! A legacy that will be remembered ​not only for the trophies or the goals, but also for the path you paved for all those who came after you. Your passion and determination to represent our country is something I’ll never forget and that will stay with me forever. I’m immensely proud of everything you’ve done for our national team! Thank you, idol."

Pepe (Former Portugal and Real Madrid defender) "It was more than just soccer. Thanks for everything, Cris."

Gianni Infantino, Fifa president "Few players have ever ​touched the heart of football fans ​around the world quite like Cristiano. A career defined by extraordinary talent, relentless determination and ​an unwavering desire to ‌push the boundaries ​of what is possible … Cristiano has ​achieved milestones that may never be matched but his greatest legacy goes far beyond records, trophies and goals … Thank you, Cristiano, for the passion, the unforgettable moments and the immense contribution you have made to our beautiful game proudly wearing the 'Selecao' shirt. Your international career will forever be part of football’s history." Reuters

Ronaldo hung around at Euro 2024, weeping after missing a penalty against Slovenia, the magnitude of his fame and ego warping perception so everything became about him, no matter how many other hugely gifted players were in that squad. And implausibly he was still doing it at the World Cup this summer: gumming the mechanisms, constantly demanding the ball, occasionally drifting out to the left to get in Rafael Leão’s way. At one point against Spain in what turns out to have been his final World Cup game, Ronaldo was released on the break but, lacking pace, ended up having to turn back and play the ball to his full-back, the opportunity gone. There was something almost painful about seeing a player once so explosive reduced to this.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There needed to be some sort of intervention. This generation of Portuguese players, who really should be challenging for major honours and not just the Nations League, could not continue to struggle on with such an albatross around their necks. It came from Jorge Jesus, the admirably forthright 72-year-old national coach, who was appointed after the World Cup. He didn’t bring Ronaldo off the bench in the second half of a tight game Portugal ended up winning against Norway. Ronaldo insisted he had been promised minutes – but even if there had been an agreement, it would be absurd to refuse a coach the capacity to adapt to circumstance – and stormed out of the camp, an indication perhaps of how his self-regard had come to distort his judgment.

And, assuming this retirement isn’t some sort of power play to force Jesus out, that is where it ended, with a €255 (£212) fine and 30-day ban over a period in which Portugal had no games. Ronaldo will go back to the Saudi Pro League to continue his pursuit of a 1,000th goal. He has been an extraordinary player. He will be remembered as an all-time great, vying with Eusébio as the greatest Portugal player of all time, but his legacy is undoubtedly tainted by this protracted farewell, by the sense that a player who at his best could win games single-handed, came by the end to be a burden to his national team. His has been a great career, but it would have been greater had it been a little shorter.
